subject: Combined Science
topic: Biology: Transport in Plants and Humans
content: Living organisms need transport systems to move nutrients, gases, and waste. 1. Transport in Plants: - Xylem: Dead tissue that transports water and minerals from the roots upwards to the leaves. This is driven by 'Transpiration Pull'—as water evaporates from the leaves (stomata), more is pulled up due to cohesion. - Phloem: Living tissue that transports manufactured food (sucrose) from leaves to the rest of the plant. This process is called 'Translocation'. 2. Transport in Humans (The Circulatory System): - The Heart: A muscular pump with 4 chambers. Deoxygenated blood enters the Right Atrium (via Vena Cava) -> Right Ventricle -> Lungs (via Pulmonary Artery). Oxygenated blood returns to Left Atrium (via Pulmonary Vein) -> Left Ventricle -> Body (via Aorta). The left ventricle has a thicker wall because it pumps blood at high pressure to the whole body. - Blood Vessels: Arteries (thick, elastic walls, carry blood under high pressure), Veins (thin walls, have valves to prevent backflow), and Capillaries (one-cell thick walls for rapid gas/nutrient exchange). 3. Blood Composition: Plasma (liquid), Red Blood Cells (oxygen transport), White Blood Cells (immunity), and Platelets (clotting).

subject: Combined Science
content: The Periodic Table is organized to show patterns in element behavior. 1. Group 1 (Alkali Metals: Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs): - Physical: Soft (can be cut with a knife), low density, low melting points. - Chemical: Highly reactive with water, producing hydrogen gas and an alkaline solution (hydroxide). - Trend: Reactivity INCREASES as you go down the group because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and easier to lose. 2. Group 7 (Halogens: F, Cl, Br, I): - Physical: Diatomic molecules (e.g., Cl2). Exist in various states (Chlorine is gas, Bromine is liquid, Iodine is solid). - Chemical: React with metals to form halides. - Trend: Reactivity DECREASES as you go down the group because it becomes harder to attract an electron into the shell further from the nucleus. - Displacement Reactions: A more reactive halogen will displace a less reactive one from its salt (e.g., Chlorine + Potassium Bromide -> Potassium Chloride + Bromine). 3. Group 0 (Noble Gases): Chemically inert (unreactive) because they have full outer shells. Uses: Helium in balloons, Neon in signs, Argon in lightbulbs.

subject: Combined Science
topic: Physics: Heat Transfer and Thermal Properties
content: Thermal energy (heat) always moves from hotter regions to colder regions. 1. Methods of Heat Transfer: - Conduction: Transfer through solids by vibration of particles and free electrons (in metals). Metals are the best conductors. - Convection: Transfer through liquids and gases by the movement of the fluid itself. Hot fluid rises (less dense), cold fluid sinks, creating 'Convection Currents'. - Radiation (Infrared): Transfer through vacuum or air by electromagnetic waves. All hot objects emit radiation. Dull black surfaces are the best emitters and absorbers, while shiny silver surfaces are the best reflectors. 2. States of Matter and Energy: - Specific Heat Capacity: The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1kg of a substance by 1C. - Latent Heat: The energy used to change state (e.g., melting ice or boiling water) without changing the temperature. 3. Expansion: Most substances expand when heated and contract when cooled. Applications: Bimetallic strips in thermostats. Exceptions: Water is most dense at 4C and expands as it freezes, which is why ice floats and pipes burst in winter.

subject: Combined Science
content: Organic chemistry focuses on carbon compounds derived from living things or petroleum. 1. Alkanes (Saturated Hydrocarbons): General formula CnH2n+2. They are used primarily as fuels. Methane (CH4) is the main component of natural gas. They are chemically unreactive except for burning in oxygen (Combustion) to produce CO2 and H2O. 2. Alkenes (Unsaturated Hydrocarbons): General formula CnH2n. They contain a C=C double bond. This makes them more reactive. They can undergo 'Addition Reactions'. For example, reacting Ethene with Bromine water will decolorize it (test for unsaturation). 3. Alcohols (Ethanol): Produced by the 'Fermentation' of sugar (glucose) using yeast at about 37C in anaerobic conditions. Equation: Glucose -> Ethanol + Carbon Dioxide. Ethanol is used as a solvent, fuel, and in alcoholic drinks. 4. Fractional Distillation of Crude Oil: A physical process that separates oil into fractions like Petrol (fuel for cars), Paraffin (jet fuel/stoves), and Diesel (trucks) based on their boiling point ranges. 5. Cracking: Breaking down long-chain alkanes into smaller, more useful molecules (like petrol and ethene) using heat and a catalyst.

subject: Combined Science
content: Mechanics is the study of motion and its causes. 1. Newton's Laws of Motion: - First Law (Inertia): An object stays at rest or in constant motion unless a force acts on it. - Second Law: Force = Mass x Acceleration (F=ma). - Third Law: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. 2. Work, Energy and Power: - Work Done (J): Force x Distance moved in the direction of the force. - Potential Energy (PE): mgh (mass x gravity x height). - Kinetic Energy (KE): 1/2 mv^2. - Power (W): The rate of doing work (Work / Time). 3. Simple Machines: Devices that make work easier by changing the magnitude or direction of a force. - Mechanical Advantage (MA): Load / Effort. - Velocity Ratio (VR): Distance moved by Effort / Distance moved by Load. - Efficiency (%): (Work Output / Work Input) x 100. No machine is 100% efficient due to 'Friction' which converts some energy into wasted heat. Examples: Levers, Pulleys, and Inclined Planes. In Zimbabwe, the 'Axe' and 'Wheelbarrow' are common simple machines used in agriculture.
